title: Fabric Operations Agent: Real-Time Monitoring and Automated Response
summary: A community/blog walkthrough of the Real-Time Intelligence Operations agent: what data it can monitor, how its detection-to-action loop is timed and gated by human approval, its concrete data-source and regional limits, and how it differs from a Fabric data agent. The post links directly to Microsoft Learn's operations-agent docs (overview, limitations, transparency note, billing) as its primary sources.
audience: SRE/DevOps and Real-Time Intelligence practitioners evaluating whether the operations agent can replace manual KQL-based alerting/runbook workflows, and architects scoping which data stores it can and cannot reach.
why_it_matters: The knowledge base currently has only one high-level operations-agent claim (from the Fabric IQ overview source). This post supplies the first concrete mechanics — polling cadence, approval-expiry window, supported/unsupported data sources, and regional availability gaps — and its outbound links (Microsoft Learn overview, limitations, transparency-note, and billing pages) are strong candidates to ingest directly as tier-1 sources.
takeaways: The operations agent runs on a fixed evaluation cadence rather than true real-time triggers, and it only reads Eventhouse/KQL data, so it cannot be pointed at lakehouse or warehouse tables directly.
Every automated action is human-in-the-loop by design: the agent proposes an action, a person approves it in Teams, and only then does Power Automate execute it under the creator's identity.
Unapproved recommendations don't linger indefinitely — they expire automatically, which matters for on-call workflows where nobody triages every alert immediately.
The feature has concrete rollout gaps (language, region, capacity tier) that make it unsuitable to assume as universally available across a Fabric tenant.

claims.text: Per the post, the Fabric Operations agent evaluates its configured detection rules against Eventhouse KQL tables on a fixed cadence of every 5 minutes, rather than reacting to events instantly as they arrive.

Per the post, the operations agent can only monitor regular KQL database tables within an Eventhouse in the same workspace as the agent, and explicitly cannot read lakehouse tables, warehouse tables, shortcut tables, KQL functions, materialized views, or columns containing nested/JSON data.

The post describes the operations agent as human-in-the-loop by design: it proposes a recommended action from its reasoning over telemetry, and a person must approve it in Microsoft Teams before a connected Power Automate flow actually executes it.
Per the post, an operations agent's proposed action that is not approved or rejected expires automatically after 3 days rather than remaining open indefinitely.
Per the post, a triggered operations-agent action executes using the identity of the person who created the agent, not the identity of whoever approves the action in Teams.

The post lists concrete rollout gaps for the operations agent at time of writing: English-language only, unavailable in the South Central US and East US regions, and unsupported on trial (non-paid) Fabric capacities.

The post places the operations agent as the reasoning stage at the end of a Real-Time Intelligence pipeline: Eventstream ingests telemetry, Eventhouse/KQL stores it, Fabric Activator applies threshold alerting, and the operations agent adds LLM-based reasoning and recommended actions on top.

The post distinguishes the operations agent from a Fabric data agent by data-source scope and mode: the data agent can query lakehouses, warehouses, KQL databases, and Power BI semantic models on demand, while the operations agent is restricted to Eventhouse/KQL sources and runs continuously rather than per-question.
